{{DISPLAYTITLE:What the axioms are}}
{{Technical|Lean theorem prover/Foundations/The three axioms|Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Classical logic from choice|Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Quotient types}}
{{Lean theorem prover map}}

Every proof Lean accepts rests on two things: the rules of Lean's logic, and
whatever '''axioms''' the proof uses, statements assumed without proof. Lean
itself provides three.<ref name="ref-axioms" /> This page says what each one says in plain
words, why the third makes Lean's logic the classical logic most mathematicians
use, and how to ask Lean which axioms a given theorem depends on.

== Rules and axioms ==

The rules of Lean's logic say how types, functions and inductive definitions
work, and how proofs are built from them. Much can be proved with these rules
alone, with no axioms at all, as the example at the end of this page shows.

An '''axiom''' is something more. In Lean it is a new constant of a given type,
simply postulated. When the type is a proposition, the axiom is an assumed proof of
it.<ref name="ref-axioms">The Lean Developers, "Axioms", ''The Lean Language Reference'', for Lean 4.35.0, chapter 8. [https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.35.0/Axioms/ lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.35.0/Axioms/] (accessed 13 October 2026).</ref> That makes axioms dangerous. Lean cannot check that an
axiom is consistent with the rest of the logic, and an axiom that is false lets
every statement be proved. Any proof that relies on an axiom is only as good as the
axiom.<ref name="ref-axioms" />

For this reason Lean keeps track of the axioms beneath every theorem, so that they
can be audited.<ref name="ref-axioms" /> And the three that Lean provides are
well studied; Lean's reference manual describes them as known to be
consistent.<ref name="ref-axioms" />

== Propositional extensionality ==

The first axiom, '''propositional extensionality''' (Lean's name is
<code>propext</code>), says: '''if two propositions imply each other, they are
equal'''.<ref name="tpil-axioms">Jeremy Avigad, Leonardo de Moura, Soonho Kong and Sebastian Ullrich, with contributions from the Lean Community, ''Theorem Proving in Lean 4'', chapter 12, "Axioms and Computation", online book for Lean 4.33.0. [https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/Axioms-and-Computation/ lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/Axioms-and-Computation/] (accessed 13 October 2026).</ref>

In plain words, a proposition is identified by when it is true, not by how it is
worded. "''p'' and true" holds in exactly the cases where ''p'' holds, so by this
axiom it is the same proposition as ''p'', and one may be replaced by the other
anywhere. This fits the reading of a proposition as a type that is either empty,
when it is false, or has a single element, when it is true.<ref name="tpil-axioms" />
It is also acceptable to constructive mathematicians.<ref name="ref-props">The Lean Developers, "Propositions", ''The Lean Language Reference'', for Lean 4.35.0, section 4.2, entry for <code>propext</code>. [https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.35.0/The-Type-System/Propositions/ lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.35.0/The-Type-System/Propositions/] (accessed 13 October 2026).</ref>

== Quotient soundness ==

The second axiom concerns '''quotients'''. A quotient is a new type made from an
old one by declaring some of its values to count as the same. The fractions 1/2
and 2/4 are different pairs of numbers but the same rational number; the numbers 3
and 10 are different, but the same when counting in sevens. The page on
[[Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Quotient types|quotient types]] treats the
construction.

Lean's logic provides the construction itself. The axiom, '''quotient
soundness''' (<code>Quot.sound</code>), supplies the one fact that makes it a real
quotient: '''values declared to count as the same become equal in the
quotient'''.<ref name="tpil-axioms" />

A useful consequence follows from it: '''function extensionality''', the principle
that two functions giving equal results on every input are equal. In Lean this is a
theorem proved from quotients, not a separate axiom.<ref name="tpil-axioms" />

== Choice ==

The third axiom, '''choice''' (<code>Classical.choice</code>), says: '''from the
bare knowledge that a type has at least one value, one may obtain a value of
it'''.<ref name="tpil-axioms" />

In plain words: if you know that something exists, you may name one, without
saying how to find it. Mathematicians use this freely. For a program it is
strange, because the knowledge that something exists, being a proof, carries no
information about where to look. The authors of ''Theorem Proving in Lean 4''
describe choice as entirely at odds with a computational reading, and Lean
requires any definition that uses it to produce data to be marked
<code>noncomputable</code>.<ref name="tpil-axioms" />

== Why choice makes the logic classical ==

Without axioms, Lean's logic is '''constructive'''. To prove "''P'' or ''Q''" one
must supply a proof of one side and say which, as the page on
[[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Propositions as types|propositions as types]]
describes. In such a logic the '''law of the excluded middle''', "every proposition
is either true or false", cannot be proved in general, because nothing tells us
which side holds.

Choice changes this. A result known as Diaconescu's theorem, after a paper by
Radu Diaconescu of 1975, shows that choice together with the two extensionality
principles proves the law of the excluded
middle.<ref name="diaconescu1975">Radu Diaconescu, "Axiom of choice and complementation", ''Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society'' 51 (1), 1975, pp. 176–178. [https://doi.org/10.1090/S0002-9939-1975-0373893-X doi:10.1090/S0002-9939-1975-0373893-X]</ref><ref name="tpil-axioms" /> Lean's core library proves it that way, and with it
the familiar classical methods: proof by contradiction, proof by cases on whether
a statement holds, and the elimination of double negation.<ref name="tpil-axioms" />
So the three axioms together give the classical logic that most of mathematics is
written in. The page on
[[Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Classical logic from choice|classical logic from choice]]
gives the proof.

The price is paid in computation, not in correctness. Proofs are dropped when
Lean compiles a program, so a program whose proofs use any of the three axioms
still runs; what Lean cannot compile is a definition that obtains data from
choice.<ref name="tpil-axioms" /><ref name="ref-axioms" /> When Lean's kernel
evaluates an expression, the axioms can also stop the evaluation before it reaches
an answer.<ref name="tpil-axioms" />

== Asking Lean ==

The command <code>#print axioms</code>, followed by the name of a theorem or
definition, lists every axiom it depends on, directly or through other theorems it
uses.<ref name="ref-axioms" /> Here are three small theorems: that "p and q"
implies "q and p"; that "p and true" is the same proposition as ''p''; and the law
of the excluded middle, taken from Lean's core library.

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
theorem swap (p q : Prop) : p ∧ q → q ∧ p := fun ⟨hp, hq⟩ => ⟨hq, hp⟩
theorem same_prop (p : Prop) : (p ∧ True) = p := propext ⟨fun h => h.1, fun h => ⟨h, trivial⟩⟩
theorem either (p : Prop) : p ∨ ¬p := Classical.em p
#print axioms swap
#print axioms same_prop
#print axioms either
</pre>

Lean 4.34.1 prints:

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
'swap' does not depend on any axioms
'same_prop' depends on axioms: [propext]
'either' depends on axioms: [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]
</pre>

The first proof uses only the rules of the logic. The second uses propositional
extensionality, by name. The third uses all three axioms, because Lean's
proof of the excluded middle goes through choice and the two extensionality
principles.

== Other names that can appear ==

The list printed by <code>#print axioms</code> is the place to look for anything
that weakens a proof.<ref name="ref-validating">The Lean Developers, "Validating a Lean proof", ''The Lean Language Reference'', for Lean 4.35.0. [https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.35.0/ValidatingProofs/ lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.35.0/ValidatingProofs/] (accessed 13 October 2026).</ref>

* <code>sorryAx</code> appears when a proof, or a theorem it relies on, is unfinished. Lean lets a proof be left open with the word <code>sorry</code> while work goes on; such a proof proves nothing.<ref name="ref-axioms" />
* A name containing <code>_native</code> means that part of the proof was settled by running compiled code, so the result also trusts Lean's compiler and not only Lean's kernel.<ref name="ref-axioms" /><ref name="ref-validating" />
* Any other name is an axiom someone added, and the theorem holds only if that axiom is true.<ref name="ref-validating" />

Lean's reference manual recommends exactly this check: a finished theorem should
report no axioms beyond the three standard ones.<ref name="ref-validating" />
Principia Machina applies the same test to its own Lean sources; see
[[Principia Machina/Lean transition|the move to Lean]].
